title: How do I write that in Rayner?
answer: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees

checks.question: Run the code-edits recipe twice in one step: count += 1 becomes count += 2, then count += 3, each morph with markAdded. What does a reader who opens that step from a link see, and is there any sign of count += 2?
checks.answer: Two lines, let count = 0 and count += 3, with count += 3 marked as added. The second morph fades count += 2 out along with its mark, so nothing in the resting picture shows that it existed; to keep it, draw the earlier panel beside the result, as the before panels on this page do.

checks.question: In the camera case, the author also enters a second circle at (5, 0) before calling s.focus(subject). Is it in the result picture, and where is it?
checks.answer: It is out of the picture. The closer view frames 6 of the stage’s 16 units around the first circle, roughly x = −3 to 3, so a circle at x = 5 falls outside it. It is still at (5, 0), because s.focus moves only the camera, and s.focus(‘all’) would bring it back into view.

checks.question: An author wants the chart case to plot numbers that each reader types into a box. Can a Rayner page do that, and what can the author offer instead?
checks.answer: No. A reader can only choose among the options a setting declares, and the build makes one case per option before anyone reads the page. The author can declare a setting whose options are a few prepared data sets, so each one is a case the build makes and the author can read.

steps.title: How do I give an idea its own link and picture?
steps.line: Predict: what address would a link to this step end with?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. this.step names a picture and its caption. The entered Text becomes that step’s resting state; the name hello gives a link an address. The empty frame is a separate comparison showing the state before entry.

steps.title: An empty step, then the greeting
steps.line: This picture and its caption are all a reader gets from a link ending ?step=hello.
steps.caption: A link to hello opens the finished greeting without playing its entry. The caption and resting picture therefore carry the explanation a direct visitor receives.

steps.title: How do I let a reader switch between prepared cases?
steps.line: Predict: which case is this page showing, and how many did the build make?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. settingsOf(this) supplies the selected option while construct builds its case. The two listed options are examples from this page’s feature picker; the result compares the default with the selected case.

steps.title: The default case, then the case you chose
steps.line: The default case is Animations; this page is the Settings case.
steps.caption: The feature picker switches between prepared cases. It changes which picture the scene builds, rather than accepting arbitrary new program input.
steps.picture: Before: the default case, feature = animation; 1 labelled value; 2 labelled values.

steps.title: How do I trace a path through a flowchart?
steps.line: Predict: once the walk ends, what stays on the flowchart?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.show uses diagram geometry captured at build time. d.walk follows the existing Start → Finish edge; trail keeps that route marked after the token finishes. The unmarked copy supplies the starting comparison.

steps.title: A bare flowchart, then its walked edge marked
steps.line: The trail stays on Start → Finish after the walk ends.
steps.caption: The trail follows a captured edge rather than drawing a shortcut. Its persistent mark makes the route inspectable after the moving token has gone.
steps.picture: Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link; Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link; Before: the captured flowchart, no path marked. Travelled: Start → Finish.

steps.title: How do I point at one line of code?
steps.line: Predict: once the focus ends, is any line still marked?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.code displays the lines; focus(1) marks the second as an update. The unmarked copy beside it makes the added emphasis visible without replaying the motion.

steps.title: Two plain lines, then the second marked as the update
steps.line: The update bar stays on count += 1 after the motion stops.
steps.caption: The update bar remains on the second line after focus finishes. That persistent mark connects the caption to the code it explains.
steps.picture: Before: the two lines, nothing marked; Code, 2 lines; Code, 2 lines. Update: 2: count += 1.

steps.title: How do I show an edit without redrawing the code?
steps.line: Predict: after the morph, which line carries the added mark?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. morph keeps the unchanged first line and replaces the increment line. markAdded identifies the replacement; the separate original panel retains the previous version.

steps.title: count += 1 edited to count += 2, the new line marked
steps.line: Only count += 2 carries the added mark; let count = 0 kept its place.
steps.caption: The surviving first line stays put while the replacement becomes current. The added mark describes the new line; it is not a history of earlier edits.
steps.picture: Before: count += 1; Code, 2 lines; Code, 2 lines. Added: 2: count += 2.

steps.title: How do I show one shape turning into another?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, do these lines leave the circle, the square or both?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Transform reshapes the object already on stage toward a target. Once finished, that object is a square. The left-hand circle is a separate starting copy, not something Transform leaves behind.

steps.title: A circle before, the square it became after
steps.line: From a link, these lines leave a square; the circle is a separate drawing.
steps.caption: Only the square comes from the recipe. The separate circle preserves the starting shape so a direct visitor can inspect the change without seeing it play.
steps.picture: Before: a circle; After: the circle has become a square.

steps.title: How do I change a label and keep its shared letters?
steps.line: Predict: from cache miss to cache hit, which letters move rather than fade?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. TransformMatchingText pairs equal characters, moves those pairs and fades unmatched glyphs. The retained old text and the correspondence list expose that mechanical rule.

steps.title: cache miss becomes cache hit
steps.line: The shared letters slid into place, and the others faded.
steps.caption: The list records the pairs the animation actually used. Matching follows characters, not word meanings, so the same letter can move into a different semantic context.

matched.moved: c a c h e i

after.moved: c a c h e i

steps.picture: Before: cache miss; Under cache hit: the letters moved, c a c h e i; faded in, h t; faded out, m s s; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I put an object back after a demonstration?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, would these lines show that the circle ever moved?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. saveState records points and style; Restore returns the circle to that record. The separately drawn dashed outline preserves the visited position after the circle returns.

steps.title: The circle moves away and returns to its saved place
steps.line: Without the dashed outline, the resting picture would hide the circle’s trip.
steps.caption: The circle ends where it began, so its resting state alone would conceal the trip. The dashed outline supplies the missing evidence of its intervening position.
steps.picture: Before: a circle whose state is saved; After: the circle is back at its saved place; a dashed outline marks where it moved to; A dashed outline where the circle moved to before Restore.

steps.title: How do I make a result stand out after the motion ends?
steps.line: Predict: when Circumscribe ends, is anything still drawn round 42?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Circumscribe normally removes its outline when the animation ends. keep: true preserves it, while s.keep supplies a description for the wordless mark. The unmarked copy shows the change.

steps.title: A plain 42, then 42 left in a box
steps.line: The box round 42 is still drawn once the motion ends.
steps.caption: The rectangle remains around 42 after motion stops. Its description also states what the emphasis marks for someone who does not see the animation.
steps.picture: Before: the result 42, unmarked; After: the result 42 remains in a box; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I bring the reader closer to a small subject?
steps.line: Predict: after the focus, has the circle moved, or has the view?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.focus changes the view rather than the subject’s coordinates. The ruler provides a stable reference because a second comparison panel would be inside the same moving camera.

steps.title: The same circle, seen through a closer view
steps.line: The view moved in; the circle kept its coordinates.
steps.caption: The ruler now shows only its middle. Its reduced visible span shows that the camera moved closer while the circle kept its coordinates.
steps.picture: A circle at the centre of a ruler that spans the stage from −7 to 7, numbered on its even ticks; The camera now frames 6.0 of the stage’s 16 units; the circle is still at (0, 0) with radius 0.6.

steps.title: How do I plot the model’s numbers?
steps.line: Predict: which values does the line pass through?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Axes maps data coordinates to stage positions. lineGraph joins the supplied points using that mapping, and the adjacent card retains the same values as numbers.

steps.title: Three values as numbers, then as a line on axes
steps.line: The line passes through 0, 2 and 1, each placed by the axes.
steps.caption: The plotted positions follow the supplied data and axes. Their agreement with the numeric card can be checked without estimating where an author placed the line by hand.
steps.picture: Before: the model’s three values as numbers; 3 labelled values; After: a line through values zero, two and one at x zero, one and two.

steps.title: How do I keep a label in step with the model’s state?
steps.line: Predict: after the sync, what number does the label show, and where does it come from?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. view builds a label from scene.state; sync rebuilds it after count changes. The recorded state and the separately retained starting label show what drove the new picture.

steps.title: state.count goes from 0 to 1, and the label follows
steps.line: Label and trace both read 1, because the view rebuilt the label from state.
steps.caption: Changing count alone does not explain a picture change: sync rebuilds the view from that value. The resulting label and recorded state agree because both use count.
steps.picture: Before: the view of state.count = 0; Recorded count: 1; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I name a point in the picture?
steps.line: Predict: what does the pin say, and where does it point?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.pin gives a named point a label and leader. The bare circle provides the comparison; the leader identifies which part the new word refers to.

steps.title: A bare circle, then its centre pinned
steps.line: The word centre sits at the end of a leader to the circle’s centre.
steps.caption: The leader binds centre to a location. The label can explain a geometric relationship without requiring another animation.
steps.picture: Before: a circle, nothing named; After: a circle whose centre is pinned; A pin marked “centre”.

steps.title: How do I lay out panels for a right-to-left page?
steps.line: Predict: in a right-to-left stage, where does a card placed at start go?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. direction: rtl places logical start on the right. The card’s own ltr direction independently orders its contents; the outline records where start would be on an ltr stage.

steps.title: Start, in a left-to-right stage and in this right-to-left one
steps.line: Start is on the right in this stage, yet the card still reads Count, 3.
steps.caption: The card sits on the right but still reads Count, 3. Placement direction and the order inside the card are separate choices.
steps.picture: Before: an outline on the left, where start is in a left-to-right stage; 1 labelled value; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I reveal a line as if drawn by hand?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, what is left of the pen’s motion?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.draw reveals a path along its length with a pen at the tip. The description states what the completed stroke represents; the separate endpoint markers supply a comparison.

steps.title: Two end points, then the line the pen drew between them
steps.line: Of the pen’s motion, only the finished line is left at rest.
steps.caption: The pen disappears when drawing ends, while the rising line remains. Its description carries the same geometric fact to readers who do not see the motion.
steps.picture: Before: the path’s two ends, nothing drawn; After: a rising line, drawn.
